gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the 75-gallon tank's own heat loss into a heater load. AquariumToolbox's cooling times for a 75-gallon tank at 77 °F in a 59 °F room work out to about 52 W wrapped in a blanket (17% duty on a 300 W heater), 184 W with only a glass lid (61%) and 323 W open (more than a 300 W heater can supply). That makes a wrapped tank about a 2 kWh day: the Elite 300 lasts about 31 h, the Elite 200 V2 about 24 h and the DELTA 2 Max about 22 h. With only a lid, no candidate passes about 12 h.
standout_why: I compared five pages. The Dealectric page ChatGPT cited and both ChatGPT answers pick a heater duty cycle (15–30% or 25%) with no physical basis. The Reefs.com Elite 100 V2 test used no heater. Planetfish gives a 75-gallon planted tank at 95 W but no heat loss. Colovma and ouraquariumlife only say to wrap the tank, with no numbers. The AquariumToolbox outage calculator gives the 75-gallon cooling times and a 323 W loss for an open tank, but never converts the lidded or wrapped cases into steady watts, 24-hour Wh or runtime on any power station.
decides: The heater's duty cycle comes from how well the tank is insulated, not from the shopper's guess, so insulation decides the pick before capacity does. In a 59 °F room, a blanket-wrapped tank (≈69.5 W of equipment plus the station's own draw) is covered for 24 h by the BLUETTI Elite 300, with about 7 h to spare. The Elite 200 V2 ($899) just reaches 24 h, and the DELTA 2 Max falls short at about 22 h. A tank with only a lid needs about 5.2 kWh, which no single candidate holds; the Elite 300 lasts about 12 h. An open tank loses more heat than a 300 W heater can replace, so no battery holds temperature. In a 68 °F room with only a lid, the Elite 300 lasts about 21 h. This supports the Elite 300 pick, with the condition that the tank is wrapped. It also makes the Elite 200 V2 the cheaper pick when wrapped, at $0.47 per measured usable Wh against $0.45 for the Elite 300.

findings.label: Heat stored in 75 gal of water for a 9 °F drop (77→68 °F)
findings.note: The page uses 283 L of water and 4,186 J per litre per °C. 283 × 4,186 × 5 °C ÷ 3,600 = 1,645 Wh.

findings.label: Heat loss of a 75-gal tank, open top, 77 °F water in a 59 °F room
findings.note: 323 W is the page's own figure. 323 × 24 = 7,752 Wh. That is more than a 300 W heater's full output, so no heater holds temperature. Cross-check from the 6.8 h cooling time: 1,645 ÷ 6.8 × 1.386 = 335 W, within 4% of the stated figure.

findings.label: Steady heater load, 75-gal tank with glass lid, 59 °F room
findings.value: ≈184 W (61% duty on a 300 W heater); ≈4.4 kWh per 24 h
findings.note: The page gives 12.4 h to cool from 77 to 68 °F with a glass lid. 1,645 Wh ÷ 12.4 h × 1.386 = 184 W. The 1.386 factor (18 × ln2 ÷ 9) converts the average loss during cooling into the loss at the full 18 °F gap, assuming Newtonian cooling.

findings.label: Steady heater load, 75-gal tank wrapped in a blanket, 59 °F room
findings.value: ≈52 W (17% duty on a 300 W heater); ≈1.25 kWh per 24 h
findings.note: The page gives 44 h to cool from 77 to 68 °F when wrapped. 1,645 ÷ 44 × 1.386 = 52 W. In a 68 °F room the gap halves to about 26 W (linear scaling, my estimate). Lidded in a 68 °F room scales to about 92 W.
